title: Whole Numbers
summary: Use the properties of whole numbers, divisibility rules, prime factorisation, HCF and LCM, and the order of operations to calculate accurately and solve problems.

notes.text: Sets of numbers
In Grade 8 we work with two important sets of numbers. The **natural numbers** are the counting numbers, and the **whole numbers** are the natural numbers together with zero.

notes.label: Remember
notes.text: Zero is a whole number but **not** a natural number. There is no biggest whole number: you can always add 1.
Properties of whole numbers
These properties explain why many mental calculation tricks work. Learn the names, because questions often ask which property has been used.

notes.caption: Properties of whole numbers
rows: The order of adding does not matter
The order of multiplying does not matter
The grouping when adding does not matter
The grouping when multiplying does not matter
Multiplication spreads over addition or subtraction

notes.label: Common mistake
notes.text: Subtraction and division are **not** commutative or associative. $10 - 4 = 6$ but $4 - 10 = -6$, and $(24 \div 4) \div 2 = 3$ but $24 \div (4 \div 2) = 12$.

notes.title: Worked example 1: using the properties to calculate mentally
steps: (a) Use the commutative and associative properties to pair $25$ and $4$: $(25 \times 4) \times 17 = 100 \times 17 = 1\ 700$.
(b) Write $99 = 100 - 1$ and use the distributive property: $100 \times 46 - 1 \times 46 = 4\ 600 - 46 = 4\ 554$.

notes.text: Factors, multiples and prime numbers
A **factor** of a number divides into it exactly, with no remainder. The factors of $12$ are $1;\ 2;\ 3;\ 4;\ 6;\ 12$.
A **multiple** of a number is the result of multiplying it by a natural number. The multiples of $6$ are $6;\ 12;\ 18;\ 24;\ \ldots$

A **prime number** has exactly two different factors: $1$ and itself (e.g. $2;\ 3;\ 5;\ 7;\ 11;\ 13$). A **composite number** has more than two factors (e.g. $4;\ 6;\ 9;\ 15$). The number $1$ is neither prime nor composite.

notes.label: Remember
notes.text: $2$ is the only even prime number. Every other even number has $2$ as a factor, so it has more than two factors.
**Divisibility rules** let you test for factors quickly, without dividing.

notes.caption: Divisibility rules
rows: Sum of the digits is divisible by 3
Last two digits form a number divisible by 4
Last three digits form a number divisible by 8
Sum of the digits is divisible by 9

notes.text: Prime factorisation

Every composite number can be written as a product of prime numbers in exactly one way (apart from order). To find the prime factors, keep dividing by the smallest prime that works. Write repeated factors using exponents.

notes.caption: Prime factorisation of 360 by repeated division

notes.text: Highest common factor (HCF) and lowest common multiple (LCM)
The **highest common factor** of two or more numbers is the biggest number that is a factor of all of them.
The **lowest common multiple** of two or more numbers is the smallest number that is a multiple of all of them.

items: **HCF:** multiply the prime factors that are **common** to all the numbers, using the **lowest** power of each.
**LCM:** multiply **every** prime factor that appears in any of the numbers, using the **highest** power of each.

notes.title: Worked example 2
notes.problem: Find the HCF and the LCM of $84$ and $120$.
steps: HCF: the common primes are $2$ and $3$. Lowest powers: $2^2 \times 3 = 12$.

notes.label: Exam tip
notes.text: Word problems tell you which one to use. **HCF** questions are about splitting things into the **largest equal groups** (cutting, sharing, packing). **LCM** questions are about things that **repeat** until they happen together again (buses, bells, flashing lights).

notes.title: Worked example 3: an LCM problem
notes.problem: A taxi to Soweto leaves the rank every 12 minutes and a taxi to Alexandra leaves every 15 minutes. Both leave together at 07:00. When will they next leave together?
steps: This repeats, so find the LCM of $12$ and $15$.

notes.title: Worked example 4: an HCF problem
notes.problem: A teacher has 36 pencils and 54 erasers. She wants to make identical packs with no items left over. What is the largest number of packs she can make, and what is in each pack?
steps: Splitting into the largest equal groups means HCF.
Each pack has $36 \div 18 = 2$ pencils and $54 \div 18 = 3$ erasers.
notes.answer: 18 packs, each with 2 pencils and 3 erasers

notes.text: Order of operations
When a calculation has more than one operation, work in this order, often remembered as **BODMAS**:

notes.title: Worked example 5
steps: (a) Multiply and divide first: $6 \times 4 = 24$ and $10 \div 2 = 5$. Then $18 + 24 - 5 = 37$.
(b) Brackets: $15 - 3 = 12$. Power: $12^2 = 144$. Then left to right: $144 \div 4 = 36$ and $36 \times 3 = 108$.

notes.label: Common mistake
notes.text: Division and multiplication have the **same** priority, so work from left to right. $24 \div 4 \times 2 = 6 \times 2 = 12$, not $24 \div 8 = 3$.
Rounding and estimating

To round, look at the digit just to the right of the place you are rounding to. If it is $5$ or more, round up; if it is less than $5$, round down. Estimate answers by rounding first, then check that your exact answer is close.

notes.title: Worked example 6: long multiplication and division
steps: $346 \times 20 = 6\ 920$ and $346 \times 7 = 2\ 422$; add: $6\ 920 + 2\ 422 = 9\ 342$. This is close to the estimate.

notes.text: Summary

items: Addition and multiplication are commutative and associative; multiplication is distributive over addition and subtraction.
A prime number has exactly two factors. $1$ is not prime, and $2$ is the only even prime.
Write numbers as products of primes using exponents, e.g. $360 = 2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5$.
HCF: common primes, lowest powers (sharing into groups). LCM: all primes, highest powers (things that repeat).
Order of operations: brackets, powers and roots, then × and ÷ left to right, then + and − left to right.
Estimate first, then check that your exact answer is reasonable.

questions.prompt: Which of these numbers is prime?
questions.explanation: $51 = 3 \times 17$, $57 = 3 \times 19$ and $91 = 7 \times 13$. Only $59$ has exactly two factors, $1$ and $59$.
The natural numbers start at $1$. Zero is a **whole** number ($\mathbb{N}_0$) but not a natural number.
$36 = 2^2 \times 3^2$ and $60 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 5$. Common primes with lowest powers: $2^2 \times 3 = 12$.
$12 = 2^2 \times 3$ and $18 = 2 \times 3^2$. All primes with highest powers: $2^2 \times 3^2 = 36$.
Multiply and divide first: $4 \times 3 = 12$ and $6 \div 2 = 3$. Then $20 - 12 + 3 = 11$.

questions.prompt: Match each statement with the property it shows.
questions.explanation: Commutative: order changes. Associative: grouping changes. Distributive: multiplication spreads over addition. $0$ is the identity for addition and $1$ is the identity for multiplication.
Look at the last two digits: $92 \div 4 = 23$ exactly, so $3\ 492$ is divisible by $4$.

questions.prompt: Which number is a factor of $2\ 345$?
questions.explanation: The last digit is $5$, so it is divisible by $5$. The last digit is odd (not divisible by $2$), and the digit sum $2 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 14$ is not divisible by $3$ or $9$.
The hundreds digit is $7$ and the digit to its right is $5$, so round up: $46\ 800$.
$16 \times 200 = 3\ 200$, leaving $256$, and $16 \times 16 = 256$. So the answer is $200 + 16 = 216$.

questions.prompt: Use the properties of numbers to calculate $125 \times 37 \times 8$ mentally.
$72 = 2^3 \times 3^2$. What is the smallest natural number you must multiply $72$ by to get a perfect square?
questions.explanation: A perfect square has even exponents on every prime. $3^2$ is fine, but $2^3$ needs one more $2$: $72 \times 2 = 144 = 2^4 \times 3^2 = 12^2$.

questions.prompt: Use the distributive property to calculate $99 \times 23$ without a calculator. Show your method.

(a) Write $540$ and $756$ as products of prime factors, using exponents.  (2)
(b) Hence find the HCF and the LCM of $540$ and $756$.  (3)
Bells at two schools ring at regular intervals. One rings every 18 minutes and the other every 24 minutes. Both ring at 08:00. At what time will they next ring together? Show your working.
questions.memo:
The events repeat, so use the LCM ✓ (1)
$18 = 2 \times 3^2$, $24 = 2^3 \times 3$, LCM $= 2^3 \times 3^2 = 72$ minutes ✓ (1)
08:00 + 72 min = 09:12 ✓ (1)

questions.prompt: There are 48 boys and 60 girls in Grade 8. They must be divided into groups of equal size, and each group must contain only boys or only girls. What is the largest possible group size, and how many groups will there be?
questions.memo:
Largest equal groups: use the HCF ✓ (1)
HCF of $48$ and $60$ is $12$, so groups of 12 ✓ (1)
$48 \div 12 + 60 \div 12 = 4 + 5 = 9$ groups ✓ (1)
